source.author: Anonymous (Old Norse wisdom poem, attributed to Odin)
source.work: Hávamál (The Sayings of the High One)

entries.text: A guest should depart before he becomes a burden, and the fire should be put out before it burns the house.
Cattle die, kinsmen die, you yourself must die. But one thing never dies: the reputation we leave behind.
No man is so good that he has no faults, nor so wicked that he is worth naught.
Praise no day until evening, no wife until buried, no sword until tested, no ice until crossed, no ale until drunk.
A middling wise man, that's the best: who knows enough to know he doesn't know all.
Be not a prideful guest in another's house; silent you sit, or choose words with care.
He who stands at a strange door should be cautious before crossing it.
A man's home is his castle, no matter how small.
Better gear than good sense a traveler cannot carry.
Better a live dog than a dead lion.
He who observes well and is cautious will seldom come to harm.
A path unwalked is hard to learn; a cup undrunk is hard to know.
Friends should share joys and show loyalty; gifts given in friendship make friendships last.
Never trust the words of a sick man's promises, nor the calm of a frozen lake.
Moderate and wise every man should be, and not with knowledge too keen; of those men whose lives are well lived, the hearts are seldom glad if their wisdom is overlarge.
